cases.title: Technical continuation (text only)
cases.targetUser: After the gateway v3.4 rollout, tenant acme-west is getting HTTP 429 responses well below its contracted rate. Please investigate the rate limiter, fix it, verify the fix with the rate limiter tests, and tell me exactly what is still left to do before we can ship.
cases.targetAssistant:
# acme-west 429s below quota: work log, fix and verification

## 1. Reproducing the problem
I replayed the 14:00-14:10 UTC access-log window for acme-west against a local gateway built from v3.4.0. The tenant's contract allows a sustained 5 requests per second per route with a burst capacity of 40. The replay holds 2,861 requests over 600 seconds on `POST /v2/orders`, about 4.8 requests per second, so none of them should be throttled. The local v3.4.0 gateway rejected 1,094 of them with HTTP 429. The same replay against v3.3.2 rejected none.

The rejections did not start at once. The first 40 requests passed, which matches the burst capacity. After that, most requests were rejected except the ones that arrived after a pause of a second or more. That pattern says the bucket drained and then refilled far more slowly than 5 tokens per second.

## 2. First hypothesis: clock skew between gateway nodes
v3.4 moved bucket state into Redis so that every gateway node shares one bucket per tenant and route. My first guess was that a node with a fast clock wrote `last_refill_ms` values in the future, so the next node computed a negative elapsed time and added no tokens.

I checked the NTP offsets of all six production gateway nodes in the node-exporter metrics for the incident window. The largest absolute offset was 1.7 ms. I then reproduced the problem on a single local node, where skew between nodes cannot happen. Clock skew is ruled out.

## 3. Interim mitigation I tried and then abandoned: raising burst_capacity
While I was still looking, I raised `burst_capacity` for acme-west from 40 to 80 in `config/limits.yaml` and planned to ship that as a hotfix:

```diff
   acme-west:
     rate_per_second: 5
-    burst_capacity: 40
+    burst_capacity: 80
```

With 80, the replay produced 512 rejections instead of 1,094, so it only delayed the problem. More importantly, the acme-west contract caps burst at 40, and `config/limits.yaml` is where that contract is enforced. Raising it would let the tenant exceed what they pay for once the real bug is fixed. I reverted the change. `config/limits.yaml` is back to `burst_capacity: 40` and is not part of the fix. My earlier note in the incident channel said we would ship the burst increase as a hotfix; that plan is withdrawn.

## 4. Root cause: the refill drops sub-second elapsed time
The refill code in `gateway/ratelimit/bucket.go` was rewritten for v3.4 when the state moved to Redis. `TokenBucket.refill` reads `last_refill_ms` from Redis, converts the elapsed time to whole seconds with integer division, and then resets `last_refill_ms` on every call:

```go
func (b *TokenBucket) refill(nowMs int64) {
	elapsedSec := (nowMs - b.lastRefillMs) / 1000
	b.tokens = min(b.capacity, b.tokens+elapsedSec*b.ratePerSecond)
	b.lastRefillMs = nowMs
}
```

When requests arrive less than one second apart, `elapsedSec` is 0, so no token is added, and the reset throws away the partial second that did elapse. Under steady traffic the bucket almost never refills; only a pause of a full second adds tokens. v3.3.2 kept the bucket in process memory and measured elapsed time as a fractional `time.Duration`, which is why the old version was correct. The bug is confined to the v3.4 rewrite.

## 5. The fix
The fix computes the refill from elapsed milliseconds and advances `last_refill_ms` only by the time that the whole tokens it added represent, so the remainder carries over to the next call:

```diff
--- a/gateway/ratelimit/bucket.go
+++ b/gateway/ratelimit/bucket.go
@@ -58,9 +58,15 @@ func (b *TokenBucket) refill(nowMs int64) {
-	elapsedSec := (nowMs - b.lastRefillMs) / 1000
-	b.tokens = min(b.capacity, b.tokens+elapsedSec*b.ratePerSecond)
-	b.lastRefillMs = nowMs
+	elapsedMs := nowMs - b.lastRefillMs
+	if elapsedMs <= 0 {
+		return
+	}
+	added := elapsedMs * b.ratePerSecond / 1000
+	if added > 0 {
+		b.tokens = min(b.capacity, b.tokens+added)
+		b.lastRefillMs += added * 1000 / b.ratePerSecond
+	}
+	if b.tokens == b.capacity {
+		b.lastRefillMs = nowMs
+	}
 }
```

The last branch stops a full bucket from banking refill time. A backwards clock reading (`elapsedMs <= 0`) now leaves the bucket alone instead of resetting it.

Decision on the Redis layout: I deliberately kept the key schema `rl:{tenant}:{route}`, the hash fields `tokens` and `last_refill_ms`, and the integer token type exactly as they are. During the rolling deploy, v3.4.0 nodes and fixed nodes read and write the same keys, and v3.4.0 parses `tokens` as an integer. An earlier idea of mine was to store fractional tokens as a float; I dropped it for that reason, because v3.4.0 nodes would fail to parse the new values mid-deploy.

For rates that do not divide 1000 evenly, such as 3 per second, the integer advance can drift by at most 1 ms per token. That is far below anything a tenant can observe, and `TestRefillNonDivisorRate` covers it.

## 6. Tests added
In `gateway/ratelimit/bucket_test.go` I added:
- `TestRefillSubSecondIntervals`: 200 requests at 210 ms spacing with rate 5 and burst 40 must produce zero rejections.
- `TestRefillCarriesRemainder`: three calls 150 ms apart add exactly the right token count.
- `TestRefillCapsAtCapacity` and `TestRefillNonDivisorRate`.
- `TestRefillIgnoresBackwardsClock`.
- `TestReplayAcmeWestWindow`: replays the anonymized fixture `testdata/acme_west_replay.jsonl` and expects zero rejections.
- `TestKeySchemaUnchanged`: pins the key format and hash field names so the rolling-deploy compatibility cannot regress silently.

Before the fix, the new refill tests and the replay test failed: `TestRefillSubSecondIntervals` rejected 160 of 200 requests and `TestReplayAcmeWestWindow` rejected 1,094, matching the production replay.

## 7. Verification
Command: `go test ./gateway/ratelimit/... -v -count=1`

```

--- PASS: TestAllowWithinBurst (0.00s)
```

All 23 tests pass. I also ran `go test -race ./gateway/ratelimit/... -count=1`:

```

```

What I did not test:
- Behavior against a real multi-node Redis cluster. The tests use miniredis in process.
- The staging load test, `k6 run loadtest/tenant_burst.js`. The staging gateway credentials in the vault (`staging/gateway-loadtest`) have expired and I do not have rights to rotate them, so I could not run it.

## 8. Where things stand
- Fixed: the refill arithmetic in `TokenBucket.refill` in `gateway/ratelimit/bucket.go`, with the tests above. The change is on draft PR #2214, not merged.
- Not part of the fix: `config/limits.yaml`. Burst stays at 40 per the contract; the hotfix to 80 was reverted and withdrawn.
- Unchanged on purpose: the Redis key schema and integer token fields, for compatibility with v3.4.0 nodes during the rolling deploy.
- Still to do: ask the platform team to rotate the `staging/gateway-loadtest` credentials, then run `k6 run loadtest/tenant_burst.js` against staging with the acme-west traffic profile and confirm zero 429s. Only after that, deploy the fix as a canary to 5% of acme-west traffic before the full rollout.

Separately, I attached reference-1.png: it is the reference for the region-health indicator we will build after this fix. Please interpret the attached image.
cases.targetAssistant:
# Nightly CSV export timestamps: work log, fix and verification

## 1. Reproducing the problem
I compared the nightly export file for 2026-10-09 with the source rows in the reporting database. Event 88,412,977 happened at 10:14:03 UTC, and the export file has `event_time` = `2026-10-09T21:14:03Z`. That is 11 hours late, and it is labelled as UTC. In the files for 2026-10-03 and 2026-10-04 the offset is 10 hours; from 2026-10-05 onwards it is 11 hours. The files up to and including 2026-10-02 are correct.

The change of offset on 2026-10-05 matches the start of daylight saving time in Sydney, which pointed at the worker's local time zone. The export worker hosts run with `TZ=Australia/Sydney`.

## 2. Finding the change
`git log -p reports/export/` shows that PR #881, merged on 2026-10-02 as "simplify timestamp handling", changed `format_row` in `reports/export/csv_writer.py`:

```diff
-    event_time = datetime.fromtimestamp(row.event_ts, tz=timezone.utc)
+    event_time = datetime.fromtimestamp(row.event_ts)
     out["event_time"] = event_time.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")
```

Without `tz`, `datetime.fromtimestamp` returns a naive datetime in the process's local zone, Australia/Sydney, and the format string still appends a literal `Z`. So every timestamp since the first run after that merge is local Sydney time mislabelled as UTC. The first affected nightly file is 2026-10-03 and the last is 2026-10-11, nine files in total.

## 3. First approach, abandoned: converting in SQL
My first fix converted the timestamp in the export query instead, adding `AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'` to `event_time` in `reports/export/query.sql` and formatting the database value directly. The export tests passed with it. Then I found that `query.sql` is not private to the export: `reports/api/dashboard.py` loads the same file for the dashboard's event timeline, and that code already converts to the viewer's zone. With my change, the dashboard showed every event shifted by the viewer's offset a second time. I reverted the SQL change. `query.sql` is unchanged, and the conversion now happens only where the CSV is serialized.

I also considered setting `TZ=UTC` on the worker hosts. I rejected that: the same hosts run the invoice-reminder and payroll cron jobs, which are scheduled in Sydney local time on purpose. Changing the host zone would move those jobs. The worker zone stays Australia/Sydney.

## Who consumed the bad files
Before fixing anything I checked who reads the export, because that decides how the bad files have to be repaired. The export bucket's access log for 2026-10-03 to 2026-10-11 shows two readers. The finance loader picks up each file at 06:00 Sydney time and loads it into the revenue warehouse; it validates the header row and the `event_time` format and then trusts the values, so the warehouse now holds nine days of rows with shifted times. The second reader is an ad-hoc analyst notebook that downloaded the 2026-10-07 file once. Nothing else touched the files.

The finance loader reloads a day completely when a file with the same date is replaced and the manifest marks it as regenerated, so a backfill that rewrites the nine files repairs the warehouse as well. No manual warehouse edit is needed. I confirmed this in the loader's README and in its `reload_on_manifest_change` setting, which is enabled in production.

## 4. The fix
```diff
--- a/reports/export/csv_writer.py
+++ b/reports/export/csv_writer.py
@@ -41,7 +41,7 @@ def format_row(row: ExportRow) -> dict[str, str]:
-    event_time = datetime.fromtimestamp(row.event_ts)
+    event_time = datetime.fromtimestamp(row.event_ts, tz=timezone.utc)
     out["event_time"] = event_time.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")
```

This restores the explicit UTC conversion that PR #881 removed. The output contract is unchanged: the column is still named `event_time`, it is still the first column, and the value is still ISO 8601 with a `Z` suffix and whole seconds. The downstream finance loader validates exactly that header and format, so neither may change.

I added two regression tests in `tests/export/test_csv_writer.py`:
- `test_format_row_emits_utc` runs `format_row` with the process zone forced to Australia/Sydney and checks that 10:14:03 UTC comes out as `10:14:03Z`.
- `test_format_row_dst_boundary` checks rows on both sides of the 2026-10-05 daylight-saving change.

Both fail on the code from PR #881 and pass with the fix.

## 5. Verification
Command: `pytest tests/export -v`


Not verified yet:
- The full nightly job against a production snapshot. That needs a read-replica access window, which is booked for tomorrow morning.
- The backfill. I have not regenerated any of the nine bad files.

## 6. Where things stand

# CI move from Node 20 to Node 22: work log, decisions and verification

## Version bump
- `.nvmrc`: 20.18.0 -> 22.11.0.
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml`: the `node-version` matrix is now `[22.x]` for both the x64 and the arm64 jobs, and the dependency key of `actions/setup-node` now includes the Node major version so Node 20 installs are not reused.
- `package.json`: `"engines": { "node": ">=22.11 <23" }`.

The workflow change:

```diff
--- a/.github/workflows/ci.yml
+++ b/.github/workflows/ci.yml
@@ -14,14 +14,13 @@ jobs:
     strategy:
       matrix:
         runner: [ubuntu-24.04, ubuntu-24.04-arm]
-        node-version: [20.x]
+        node-version: [22.x]
     runs-on: ${{ matrix.runner }}
     steps:
       - uses: actions/checkout@v4
       - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
         with:
           node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
-      - run: npm rebuild node-sass
       - run: npm ci
       - run: npm run build
       - run: npm test -- --ci
```

The first `npm ci` on Node 22 failed in the `node-sass` postinstall step:

```
npm error gyp info using node@22.11.0 | linux | x64
npm error Node Sass does not yet support your current environment: Linux 64-bit with Unsupported runtime (127)
npm error code 1
```

`node-sass` 7.0.5 ships no prebuilt binary for Node 22 (ABI 127), and the project is deprecated.

## First approach, abandoned: building node-sass from source
I first tried keeping `node-sass` by moving to `node-sass@9.0.0` with `npm rebuild node-sass --build-from-source`. On the x64 runner the native build took 6 minutes 40 seconds, which alone would double our CI time. On the arm64 runner it failed in `node-gyp` with an unsupported compiler flag for libsass. I dropped this approach and removed the rebuild step from the workflow.

## Decision: replace node-sass with sass
I replaced `node-sass` with `sass` 1.80.6 (Dart Sass, pure JavaScript, no native build) and pointed `sass-loader` at it with `implementation: require("sass")`. The `.scss` sources are unchanged. Two deprecated division expressions produce warnings under Dart Sass; they still compile and I left them for a separate clean-up.

The `package.json` changes:

```diff
   "scripts": {
-    "build": "NODE_OPTIONS=--openssl-legacy-provider webpack --mode production",
+    "build": "webpack --mode production",
     "test": "jest"
   },
   "devDependencies": {
-    "node-sass": "7.0.5",
+    "sass": "1.80.6",
     "sass-loader": "16.0.2",
     "webpack": "5.95.0",
```

I checked every other native dependency in the lockfile for Node 22 support before going further. There are two: `esbuild` and `fsevents`. `esbuild` 0.24 ships Node 22 binaries for both architectures, and `fsevents` is macOS-only and optional, so neither needs a change.

I did not move to Node 24. The company LTS policy keeps production and CI on Node 22 until April 2027, and this change stays inside that policy.

## Other changes the upgrade needed
- Build script: removed `--openssl-legacy-provider` from `NODE_OPTIONS` in the `build` script. It was a workaround for webpack 4's MD4 hashing; webpack 5.95 does not need it, and Node 22 prints a warning when it is set without need.
- Snapshots: two snapshots in `ui/__snapshots__/Button.test.js.snap` changed because Dart Sass emits slightly different whitespace in the inlined CSS. I diffed them; the only change is whitespace, and I accepted both.
- Warnings: Node 22 prints `DEP0040` (the `punycode` module is deprecated). It comes from a transitive dependency, `whatwg-url` via `node-fetch@2`, not from our code. It is harmless and I left it.

## Verification
Locally on Node 22.11.0, from a clean checkout:

`npm ci` completed in 41 s with no native build steps. `npm run build` succeeded: the main bundle is 1.42 MB, up from 1.41 MB on Node 20 because Dart Sass inlines a few more CSS custom-property fallbacks.
